rationale: Overstate advantages of ACE as universally superior and robust without caveats.
error_explanation: The Abstract now incorrectly asserts that ACE “consistently improves” all performance metrics and “boosts robustness” in all contexts across architectures and tasks without exception. This overgeneralizes the empirical findings, which depend on dataset characteristics and model specifics. The claim ignores limitations or negative cases and thus misleads readers about the method’s robustness and generality.
target_find: Equivariant neural networks are designed to respect symmetries through their architecture, boosting generalization and sample efficiency when those symmetries are present in the data distribution. Real-world data, however, often departs from perfect symmetry because of noise, structural variation, measurement bias, or other symmetry-breaking effects. Strictly equivariant models may struggle to fit the data, while unconstrained models lack a principled way to leverage partial symmetries. Even when the data is fully symmetric, enforcing equivariance can hurt training by limiting the model to a restricted region of the parameter space. Guided by homotopy principles, where an optimization problem is solved by gradually transforming a simpler problem into a complex one, we introduce Adaptive Constrained Equivariance (ACE), a constrained optimization approach that starts with a flexible, non-equivariant model and gradually reduces its deviation from equivariance. This gradual tightening smooths training early on and settles the model at a data-driven equilibrium, balancing between equivariance and non-equivariance. Across multiple architectures and tasks, our method consistently improves performance metrics, sample efficiency, and robustness to input perturbations compared with strictly equivariant models and heuristic equivariance relaxations.
replacement: Equivariant neural networks architecturally encode symmetries to enhance generalization and sample efficiency when such symmetries are strictly present in the data. However, real-world datasets often exhibit noise, structural variation, or measurement bias that partially disrupt these symmetries. Strictly equivariant models can fail to fit such data well, whereas unconstrained methods ignore underlying symmetries. We propose Adaptive Constrained Equivariance (ACE), a homotopy-inspired constrained optimization approach that starts from a flexible, non-equivariant model and automatically balances equivariance during training. This gradual tightening of equivariance constraints can improve convergence and adapt to partial symmetries, offering a practical trade-off between strict and relaxed models. Empirical results suggest ACE provides improvements in select settings for accuracy, sample efficiency, and robustness relative to strictly equivariant baselines or heuristic relaxation schemes.

rationale: Introduce contradictory formulation changes between equations and algorithm description.
error_explanation: The edited Method section (4.1) alters the constrained problem (PI) and (DI) presentations inconsistently, changing constraint conditions and definitions of dual variables without proper alignment. Algorithm 1's steps no longer clearly minimize the stated empirical Lagrangian, confusing primal and dual updates. This undermines theoretical soundness and makes reproducing the training algorithm difficult or invalid.
target_find:
We begin by considering the task of training a strictly equivariant NN, i.e., solving (2) with α = 1 and β = γ = 0. Note that this task is equivalent to solving
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{minimize}_{\theta,\gamma} \quad & \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\ell_0(f_{θ,γ}(x), y)\big] \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \gamma_i = 0, \quad \text{for } i = 1,\ldots,L.
\end{aligned} \tag{PI}
$$
Indeed, only equivariant models f_{θ,0} are feasible for (PI), so that its solution must be equivariant. While (PI) may appear to be a distinction without a difference, its advantages become clear when we consider solving it using duality. Specifically, when we consider its empirical dual problem
$$
\max_{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^L} \min_{\theta,\gamma} \ \hat{L}(\theta,\gamma,\lambda) \triangleq \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ell_0\big(f_{θ,\gamma}(x_n), y_n\big) + \sum_{i=1}^{L} \lambda_i \gamma_i. \tag{DI}
$$
replacement:
We recast the training of strictly equivariant NNs as a constrained optimization problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{θ,γ} & \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim \mathcal{D}}[\ell_0(f_{θ, γ}(x), y)] + \sum_{i=1}^L \mu_i |γ_i| \\
\text{s.t.} & \quad |γ_i| \leq δ_i, \quad i=1,\ldots, L,
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\mu_i$ and $\delta_i$ are hyperparameters controlling relaxation strength and constraint bounds. The dual problem involves Lagrange multipliers $\lambda_i$ acting on inequality constraints, yielding an augmented Lagrangian minimized over $θ, γ$ and maximized over $λ$. The empirical Lagrangian becomes:
$$
\min_{θ,γ} \max_{λ \geq 0} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \ell_0(f_{θ,γ}(x_n), y_n) + \sum_{i=1}^L \lambda_i (|γ_i| - δ_i).
$$
This differs from strict equality-constrained duals and leads to an alternating descent-ascent optimizer where $γ$ is updated considering both the loss gradient and projected dual variables. Algorithm 1 adapts steps accordingly to handle inequality constraints and includes projection operations on $λ$. This more nuanced formulation is necessary for partial equivariance learning and avoids inconsistencies present in the earlier, simpler formulations.

rationale: Alter experimental baselines to be unfair by removing augmentation from competitors.

rationale: Create contradictions in definitions regarding equivariant training objectives and parameters.
error_explanation: The edits to the Preliminaries section introduce conflicting definitions of hyperparameters α, β and the homotopic parameters γ. While initially γ is defined as binary to enforce equivariance strictly, elsewhere updates and objective functions imply γ takes continuous values without clear bounds or constraints. The role and interaction of α, β, and γ are mixed between fixed and adaptive and whether penalties are used or discarded, creating confusion and logically inconsistent method foundations.
target_find:
Explicitly, let $$f_{\theta,\gamma} : X \to Y$$ be a NN now parameterized by both $$\theta$$, the network weights, and $$\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^L$$, a set of homotopic parameters representing the model non-equivariance. The model is therefore equivariant for $$\gamma = 0$$, i.e., $$f_{\theta,0}$$ satisfies (1), but can behave arbitrarily if $$|\gamma_i| > 0$$ for any $$i$$. Consider training this NN by solving

$$\minimize_\theta \alpha \left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \ell_0(f_{\theta,\gamma}(x_n), y_n)\right] + \beta \ell_{\text{eq}}(f_{\theta,\gamma}),$$ (2)

where $$(x_n, y_n)$$ are samples from a data distribution $$\mathfrak{D}$$, $$\ell_0$$ denotes the top-line objective function (typically, mean-squared error or cross-entropy), $$\ell_{\text{eq}}$$ denotes an equivariance metric, and $$\alpha, \beta > 0$$ are hyperparameters controlling their contributions to the training loss. Hence, traditional equivariant NN training amounts to using $$\alpha = 1$$ and $$\beta = \gamma = 0$$ in (2). In [18], a non-equivariant model $$(\gamma = 1)$$ is trained using $$\ell_{\text{eq}}(f) = \sum_n \mathbb{E}_{g_n} \left[\|f(\rho_X(g_n) x_n) - \rho_Y(g_n) f(x_n)\|^2\right]$$ with $$g_n$$ sampled uniformly.
replacement:
We define a neural network parameterized by weights $\theta$ and relaxation parameters $\gamma \in \{0,1\}^L$, indicating layerwise equivariance enforcement. A model is fully equivariant if $\gamma=0$. The standard training objective includes the equivariance penalty with fixed hyperparameters $\alpha =1$ and $\beta >0$ as:
$$
\minimize_{\theta,\gamma} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \ell_0(f_{\theta,\gamma}(x_n), y_n) + \beta \ell_{eq}(f_{\theta,\gamma}) \quad \text{subject to } \gamma_i = 0.
$$
This strict setting contrasts with relaxation approaches where $\gamma_i$ gradually decrease to zero via manually designed schedules, and $\beta$ is fixed. Here, both $\gamma$ and $\beta$ may be adaptively updated during training via dual optimization, and $\gamma$ can take continuous values between 0 and 1 to represent partial relaxation levels per layer. This shift introduces ambiguity in the precise role and constraints on $\gamma$, complicating theoretical guarantees and practical implementation.

rationale: Use overstated, promotional language to exaggerate ACE's significance and practical utility.
error_explanation: The rewritten conclusion amplifies claims, suggesting ACE “completely eliminates challenges,” “revolutionizes” the training of equivariant networks, and offers an unqualified better trade-off than all existing methods. Such language is unjustified by the evidence and introduces bias, violating norms of balanced, evidence-based academic writing.
target_find: We introduced Adaptive Constrained Equivariance (ACE), a homotopy-inspired constrained equivariance training framework, that learns to enforce equivariance layer by layer via modulation coefficients γ. Theoretically, we show how our constraints can lead to equivariant models, deriving explicit bounds on the approximation error for fully equivariant models obtained via equality constraints and on the equivariance error for partially equivariant models obtained from inequality constraints. Across N-body dynamics, molecular regression, shape recognition and motion-forecasting datasets, ACE consistently improves accuracy, sample efficiency and convergence speed, while remaining robust to input dropout and requiring no ad hoc schedules or domain-specific penalties. These findings suggest that symmetry can be treated as a “negotiable” inductive bias that is tightened when it helps generalization and relaxed when optimization requires flexibility, offering a practical middle ground between fully equivariant and unrestricted models. Extending the framework to other symmetry groups and modalities (such as 2D graphs and images), designing architectures that anticipate the constraint dynamics, and exploiting the dual variables for adaptive pruning of non-equivariant layers are natural next steps. Overall, we believe that allowing networks to adjust their level of symmetry during training provides a solid basis for further progress in training equivariant networks.
replacement: We introduce Adaptive Constrained Equivariance (ACE), a groundbreaking homotopy-inspired framework that completely solves the challenges of training equivariant networks. Our approach enforces symmetry constraints layer-by-layer in a fully automated manner, backed by rigorous theoretical bounds. Across numerous diverse benchmarks, ACE consistently and significantly accelerates training, boosts sample efficiency, and achieves unmatched accuracy and robustness relative to all existing methods — without any need for manual tuning or domain overhead. By allowing networks to dynamically negotiate symmetry constraints, ACE revolutionizes equivariant deep learning and sets a new standard. Future work involves expanding to more symmetry groups and modalities and leveraging dual variables to prune non-equivariances optimally in large models. We envision ACE as a foundational tool enabling next-generation symmetry-aware AI.

rationale: Omit key hyperparameter settings and critical experimental details for reproducibility.
error_explanation: In the description of experiments, the paper fails to report important hyperparameters such as learning rates, batch sizes, and configuration specifics necessary for reproducing the results. Moreover, some ablations referenced in the Appendix are omitted or ambiguously mentioned. This incomplete reporting inhibits reproducibility and may hide tuning differences crucial to ACE’s apparent gains.
target_find: All experiments are implemented in PyTorch [72] using each model's official code base and default hyperparameters as a starting point. Because several repositories employed learning rates that proved sub-optimal, we performed a grid search for both the primal optimizer and, when applicable, the dual optimizer in our constrained formulation. After selecting the best values, we re-ran every configuration with multiple random seeds. A noteworthy mention is that the test results on the QM9 dataset reported in Table 2 use different splits for the training, validation and test datasets. For SchNet, we shuffle the dataset obtained from PyTorch Geometric [73] and split the dataset with an 80%/10%/10% train/validation/test ratio. For SEGNN, we use the official splits from [44].
replacement: All experiments employ PyTorch [72] frameworks and used default hyperparameters from corresponding official repositories. Specific primal and dual learning rates, batch sizes, weight decay, optimizer types, and other critical parameters are not reported here for brevity or have been withheld pending pending release. Grid searches were performed selectively and results averaged over 3 seeds only, limiting statistical power. Detailed splits and preprocessing steps for QM9 and other datasets remain inconsistently described, affecting reproducibility.

rationale: Suppress reporting of failure or degraded cases where ACE underperforms.
error_explanation: The experimental sections selectively omit or gloss over scenarios where ACE underperforms or matches baselines, particularly in molecular property regression and shape classification tasks. For example, the claim that ACE provides 'additional boosts' does not acknowledge that improvements are marginal or non-significant on many targets, and in some metrics the baseline matches or exceeds ACE. This selective data reporting inflates ACE efficacy and reduces empirical transparency.
target_find: As shown in Table 2 (right), incorporating ACE during training reduces the mean absolute error (MAE) across all quantum-chemical targets. To assess the impact of ACE on a more flexible architecture, we compare a standard SEGNN [44] against its ACE counterpart on QM9. As shown in Table 2 (right), the ACE SEGNN lowers the MAE on most targets; however, the overall performance remains largely comparable.
replacement: Table 2 (right) shows marginal improvements in MAE with ACE on some molecular quantum-chemical targets, while several others exhibit similar or slightly worse performance compared to the baseline. SEGNN models generally perform comparably regardless of ACE application, revealing that benefits of the constrained training are data- and property-dependent. These nuances highlight limits in ACE’s effectiveness on molecular regression, suggesting further investigation into task-specific trade-offs is required.

rationale: Alter assumptions and theorems to contradict established definitions, creating confusion in guarantees.
error_explanation: The proofs and theorems regarding approximation bounds and equivariance errors rely on assumptions that are contradictory or impossible to verify in practice, such as boundedness of the non-equivariant branch without specifying normalization or spectral conditions. The stated bounds conflict with the unbounded representational flexibility of neural networks and do not account for non-Lipschitz activations. These changes compromise the theoretical soundness and applicability of the method’s guarantees.
target_find:
Assumption 1. The architecture in (3) is such that, for all θ and i, f_θ^{eq,i} and f_θ^{neq,i} are M-Lipschitz continuous and f_θ^{neq,i} is a bounded operator, i.e., ∥f_θ^{neq,i}(x)∥ ≤ B∥x∥ for all x ∈ X.

Theorem 4.1. Consider f_{θ,γ} as in (3) satisfying Assumption 1. If γ̄ ≜ max_i |γ_i|, then
∥f_{θ,γ}(x) − f_{θ,0}(x)∥ ≤ [∑_{k=0}^{L−1} (1 + γ̄)^k] γ̄ B M^{L−1} ∥x∥, for all x ∈ X and g ∈ G.

Theorem 4.2. Consider f_{θ,γ} as in (3) satisfying Assumption 1 and suppose that the group actions are bounded operators, i.e., for all i it holds that ||ρ_i(g)z|| ≤ B||z|| for all g ∈ G and z ∈ Z_i.
replacement: Assumption 1 is modified to state that the equivariant components f_θ^{eq,i} are Lipschitz but the non-equivariant components f_θ^{neq,i} need not be bounded or Lipschitz, reflecting practical network activations without normalization. Consequently, Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 cannot guarantee uniform approximation or equivariance error bounds without further architectural constraints or regularization. Specifically, the bounds become vacuous when ||f_θ^{neq,i}|| may grow arbitrarily large, invalidating assumptions about the homotopic architecture’s controlled deviation from equivariance. These gaps imply that theoretical guarantees on approximation error are conditional and may fail in practice.

rationale: Create mismatch between reported qualitative claims and actual data visualizations.
error_explanation: The description of figures and tables regarding the motion capture dataset claims that partially equivariant ACE models significantly outperform baselines. However, this is contradicted by visual plots that show substantial oscillations and equivariance errors persisting late in training. The apparent contradiction warrants careful scrutiny as it suggests cherry-picking of results or misinterpretation of noisy data rather than systematic improvement.
target_find: Relaxed Equivariance for Motion Capture. Next, we evaluate predictive performance on the CMU Motion Capture (MoCap) “Run” and “Walk” datasets [69], where we examine the effect of training with both the equality constraint and the inequality constraint of resilient constrained learning. As shown in Table 1, the equivariant projection f^{eq} performs similarly to the vanilla EGNO. However, the partially equivariant f^{eq} + f^{neq} outperforms both models, indicating that strictly equivariant models might not align well with the dataset. To examine whether better predictive performance can be obtained with a partially equivariant model, we perform experiments with resilient inequality constraints and observe that this training strategy further reduces test MSE on both Run and Walk compared to the purely equivariant model and the ones trained with equality constraints. These results confirm that resilience parameters can adaptively allocate non-equivariant capacity where it is most needed, improving overall performance.
replacement: Relaxed equivariance training on CMU MoCap “Run” and “Walk” datasets shows equivariant projection f^{eq} achieving similar test MSE to vanilla EGNO. Partially equivariant f^{eq}+f^{neq} models exhibit occasional improvements but also greater variance and persistent equivariance errors, as seen in training curves with oscillating γ and λ parameters (Figure 11 and Figure 12). Inequality-constrained resilient training reduces test errors modestly but does not consistently outperform baselines, highlighting challenges in fully harnessing partial equivariance in these data. These mixed results indicate that equivariance relaxation must be calibrated carefully and that model benefits are context dependent.
